newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Vranitzky tries to solve Albanian vote impasse.
newsitem.headline: Vranitzky tries to solve Albanian vote impasse.

text.p: European envoy Franz Vranitzky made a final effort on Friday to resolve an impasse over early general elections aimed at restoring normality in Albania.
Vranitsky met leaders from Albania's 10 political parties to try to thrash out a compromise on the number of seats to be chosen by proportional representation in the election, due on June 29.
"We are hopeful that our proposal will offer them a possibility to reach a compromise," Vranitzky's spokeswoman told Reuters.

She conceded that Friday was crunch day for the European team trying to break through the obstacles to the early election, agreed by the nine-party National Reconciliation government set up in March to halt Albania's slide towards chaos.

It is Vranitzky's third visit since widespread rioting over failed pyramid savings schemes broke out in February. A former Austrian chancellor, he is now acting as envoy of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE).
Formidable stumbling blocks remain to the elections.

President Sali Berisha's Democratic Party is refusing to back down on its insistence that the existing electoral law, which allows for 25 seats in the 140-seat parliament to be chosen by proportional representation, be used for the June vote.
The democrats won 122 seats in the last election in May 1996. International observers said the result was seriously flawed and the opposition Socialists pulled out of the ballot late on polling day.

The Socialists led by interim Prime Minister Bashkim Fino, as well as the other seven parties in the National Reconciliation Government, want a variation of the 1992 election law in which 40 seats were chosen by proportional representation.
The 15 seats at issue would most likely go to minor parties in the government.

Fino has said the government will now adopt an electoral law by majority and pass it to parliament for approval. He has demanded a vote of confidence, and says the government will resign if the law is not passed.

Berisha also insists the presence of "rebel committees", groups he says are the armed wing of the leftist opposition, are obstructing free elections. He wants them disbanded before the vote goes ahead, and has told the OSCE and Council of Europe to go and check on the groups and report back.
Fino has denied his Socialist party has anything to do with the salvation committees that Berisha calls rebels, and says they should be disbanded after a date is set for the elections.
The influence of the committees, citizens' groups that sprung up in southern Albania to restore order after the riots, is on the wane in much of the region.
The groups themselves deny they have any political motives, other than the return of money lost in the funds and the resignation of Berisha who they blame for the pyramids fiasco.
Fino's spokesman said the prime minister would leave Tirana on Saturday for an official visit to Washington, stopping in Rome on the way to meet Italian Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini.

A hand grenade was thrown during the night at the Tirana offices of the Soros Foundation, a body funding the development of democracy in Eastern Europe set up by the Hungarian-born U.S. financier George Soros.
No one was injured in the blast, which damaged a vehicle outside the building.
